summary: Dedicated pool: transient GPU scarcity caused by sidecar IO bursts leading to transparent fallback routing and throughput degradation
description:
Issue summary: BrightWave reported repeated throughput drops and elevated p99 latencies for their dedicated pool in us-west-2 between 2026-03-12T08:15 and 2026-03-12T11:00 UTC. Affected requests experienced transparent fallback routing to smaller model variants or queued for extended periods. Customer observed a 3x increase in tail latency and occasional 429/5xx errors during the window.
Impact: Customer's ingestion pipeline (approx 1.2k concurrent short-streams) saw degraded SLA behavior; customer revenue impact reported (ingestion backlog).
Environment: Dedicated pool (BrightWave-reserved, region us-west-2), production, pinned model redwood/gpt-small-16k (pinned v2026-02-05).
Hypothesis summary: Background sidecar process (internal telemetry/trace collector) emitted periodic microbursts of NVMe writes and small socket bursts that saturated storage I/O and caused allocator heartbeats to delay. The autoscaler misinterpreted delayed allocator heartbeats as lower utilization and delayed scale-up for ~90s windows; allocator then returned many attach failures and the routing layer performed transparent fallback to smaller/cheaper model variants causing higher tail latency and occasional 429s.
Why this is unique: Unlike classic noisy-tenant CPU/GPU hogging, the root was a high-frequency storage IO microburst from a sidecar in the same host slice that produced subtle NVMe completion queue pressure leading to attach delays (not immediate GPU OOMs). This manifested as 'GPU scarcity' from the scheduler's perspective without clear GPU driver errors.
steps_to_reproduce:
1) Deploy a high-frequency small-write telemetry sidecar on a dedicated host slice (simulate many small 4KB batched writes every 50ms).
2) Run ~1k concurrent short inference streams against a pinned model with continuous prefetch enabled.
3) Observe allocator attach latency histogram; check NVMe io wait (iowait) and completion queue metrics.
4) Correlate autoscaler metrics (heartbeat_interval, attach_fail_rate) with routing fallback events.
Expected: allocator heartbeats remain stable, autoscaler scales; no transparent fallbacks.
Observed: heartbeat delays of 60-120s, autoscaler hesitation, routing fallbacks and p99 spike.

investigation_notes:
- Initial customer repro and SLO graphs collected by Support.
- Correlated allocator missing-heartbeat spikes with NVMe write latency (nvme_lat_p99 increased from 2ms -> 60ms during windows).
- Observed sidecar flush cycles aligned with heartbeat gaps; sidecar process was writing small compressed traces every 30-60ms.
- Autoscaler uses heartbeat-derived signals and a 30s smoothing window; delayed heartbeats caused autoscaler to under-provision for ~60-120s bursts.
- No driver-level GPU errors (no dmesg GPU pagefaults), no GPU memory pressure; scheduler reported attach failures due to timeouts rather than OOM.
- Affected requests were predominantly short streams (<200 tokens). Those patterns amplify attach/detach overhead and expose prefetch/kv-cache sensitivity.
- Reproduced locally in staging using a synthetic sidecar that emits frequent small writes.
- Related internal INT ticket opened for allocator heartbeat resilience improvements.
workaround:
Short-term: customer advised to disable the telemetry sidecar flush aggregation and switch to periodic larger-compressed writes (reduce write frequency), or move sidecar to a separate host-affinity group. Support applied a temporary routing policy: increased attach timeout threshold for BrightWave's pool and raised autoscaler aggressiveness (reduced smoothing to 10s) for the dedicated slice. These changes reduced fallback events but are not permanent.
Operational note: instruct customers to avoid high-frequency small NVMe writes on hosts hosting GPU slices until fix is rolled out.
resolution_notes:
Mitigation completed 2026-03-13: rolled combined fix in three parts: 1) short-term autoscaler parameter change rolled to affected pool (aggressiveness + attach timeout) to reduce transparent fallbacks; 2) platform ops applied a host-level I/O cgroup limit to sidecar processes for isolated pools; 3) engineering PR #1284 queued to add heartbeat fallback detection logic to autoscaler and detect NVMe iowait anomalies as a separate signal for scaling.
Post-mortem planned: add to weekly oncall review; recommend adding NVMe iowait alerts to pool health dashboards and a gating check before allowing host-local sidecars on dedicated slices.
Customer follow-up: BrightWave accepted the temporary mitigations and requested timeline for permanent autoscaler logic change (target: 2 weeks).
